subtoc.Name: git maintenance start
subtoc.short_description: Runs a cronJob in background for the specified repo for periodic maintenance.
subtoc.long_description: `git maintenance start` enables background maintenance tasks for your Git repository. It sets up scheduled jobs (using your system’s scheduler, like cron on Unix or Task Scheduler on Windows) to automatically run Git maintenance commands at regular intervals. This keeps your repository fast and healthy by running tasks like garbage collection, commit-graph optimization, and cleanup operations in the background, so you don’t have to remember to do it manually.

examples.description: Enable background maintenance for your repository.
Run maintenance tasks every hour for more active repos.

steps: Run `git maintenance start` in your repository.
Optionally, use `--schedule=hourly` or `--schedule=daily` to control how often maintenance runs.
Git will now automatically run tasks like garbage collection, pruning unreachable objects, and optimizing internal data structures in the background.
You can stop background maintenance with `git maintenance stop` if needed.
subtoc.author: mike-rambil
protips: Set up maintenance on large or long-lived repos to keep them fast and healthy.
Use with cron or scheduled tasks for automation.
If you notice Git getting slow, check if maintenance is enabled or run it manually.

subtoc.Name: git request-pull
subtoc.short_description: Generate a request to pull changes into a repository.
subtoc.long_description: `git request-pull` generates a summary message describing the changes between two commits, which you can send to a project maintainer to request that they pull your changes. This is especially useful for email-based workflows or when collaborating outside of platforms like GitHub. The command outputs a message that includes a comparison summary, a list of commits, and their messages, making it easy for maintainers to review and apply your changes.

  Some previous commit message

are available in the Git repository at:

  https://github.com/example/repo.git feature-branch

for you to fetch changes up to 89abcde... (feature-branch):

  New feature commit message
  Another commit message

----------------------------------------------------------------
 file1.txt | 10 ++++++++++
 file2.js  |  5 +++++
 2 files changed, 15 insertions(+)

Request a pull for a feature branch based on main.

Send the generated message to the project maintainer (e.g., via email or chat).

Name: Commit Ranges & Push-Safety Checks
short_description: Know exactly what you're about to push (or pull) using `git status -sb` and the `..` / `...` range operators.
long_description:
When other people (or other terminals, CI bots, or AI agents) push to the same branch, "just push" is how surprises happen. Git's range syntax answers the questions you should ask first:

- **Am I ahead, behind, or both?** → `git status -sb`
- **Which commits will `git push` send?** → `git log origin/main..main`
- **Which commits would `git pull` bring in?** → `git log main..origin/main`
- **How far apart are we, and on which side?** → `git log --left-right origin/main...main`
- **What did *my* branch change since it diverged?** → `git diff origin/main...main`

The one rule to remember: **`A..B` means "what B has that A doesn't"**, and `A...B` means "what either side has that the other doesn't" (for `log`) or "B's changes since it split from A" (for `diff`). `log` and `diff` interpret the dots differently, which is why this topic trips people up.

The examples below use a real diverged repo: you made 3 local commits (`L1`–`L3`) on `main` while a teammate pushed 2 commits (`O1`, `O2`) to `origin/main`.
author: mike-rambil
protips: Always `git fetch` first. `origin/main` is only as fresh as your last fetch, so every range check against it can be stale.
Read `A..B` out loud as "from A up to B": the commits you'd have to add to A to reach B.

subtoc.Name: git status -sb: Ahead/Behind at a Glance
subtoc.short_description: One line that tells you whether a push will succeed and how many commits it carries.
subtoc.long_description:
`git status -sb` combines two flags: `-s` (short format, one line per changed file) and `-b` (show a branch header). The header compares your branch to its upstream:

```
## main...origin/main [ahead 3]            # you have 3 commits to push
## main...origin/main [behind 2]           # remote has 2 commits you don't
## main...origin/main [ahead 3, behind 2]  # diverged: both sides have new commits
## main...origin/main                      # in sync (as of your last fetch)
```

**Why check before pushing?** If someone else pushed to the same branch, you're *behind*, and a plain `git push` is rejected as non-fast-forward. You have to pull (merge or rebase) first. If you're only *ahead N*, the push is a fast-forward and will send exactly those N commits.

Real output from the demo repo: the header says `[ahead 3]` until you fetch, then the truth appears:

```
$ git status -sb
## main...origin/main [ahead 3]
$ git fetch origin
$ git status -sb
## main...origin/main [ahead 3, behind 2]
$ git push
hint: Updates were rejected because the tip of your current branch is behind
hint: its remote counterpart. If you want to integrate the remote changes,
hint: use 'git pull' before pushing again.
```

flags.-s: Short format: one line per changed file (`--short`).
flags.-b: Show the branch and its ahead/behind counts vs. upstream (`--branch`).

examples.description: Refresh remote-tracking refs, then show ahead/behind.
Script-friendly counts: prints `<behind> <ahead>` (e.g. `2` and `3`).

warnings: The counts compare against your *local copy* of `origin/main`. Without a fetch, `behind` can read 0 even when the remote has moved.
subtoc.author: mike-rambil

subtoc.Name: git log A..B: What B Has That A Doesn't
subtoc.short_description: Two-dot log lists commits reachable from B but not from A.
subtoc.long_description:
`git log A..B` shows commits reachable from `B` that are **not** reachable from `A`. In other words, "what B has that A doesn't", or "what A needs to catch up to B". It is shorthand for `git log ^A B`.

Flip the sides to flip the question:

```
$ git log --oneline origin/main..main     # what `git push` will send
dd4a108 L3: tweak feature.txt
79c2ff7 L2: edit app.txt
74bf8a1 L1: add feature.txt

$ git log --oneline main..origin/main     # what `git pull` would bring in
bf35bd9 O2: teammate updates teammate.txt
e990b1a O1: teammate adds teammate.txt
```

Omitting one side defaults it to `HEAD`: `git log origin/main..` is the same as `git log origin/main..HEAD`.

examples.description: Commits your push will send.
Commits a pull would bring in.
Same as the first, using your branch's upstream (`@{u}`) and HEAD.

subtoc.author: mike-rambil

subtoc.Name: git log A...B: Symmetric Difference with --left-right
subtoc.short_description: Three-dot log lists commits on either side but not both. Add --left-right to see which side.
subtoc.long_description:
`git log A...B` shows the **symmetric difference**: commits reachable from `A` or `B`, but not from both (i.e. everything after their merge base, on both sides). On its own the output doesn't say which side a commit came from, so pair it with `--left-right`:

- `<` marks a commit only in `A` (the left side)
- `>` marks a commit only in `B` (the right side)

```
$ git log --oneline --left-right origin/main...main
< bf35bd9 O2: teammate updates teammate.txt
> dd4a108 L3: tweak feature.txt
< e990b1a O1: teammate adds teammate.txt
> 79c2ff7 L2: edit app.txt
> 74bf8a1 L1: add feature.txt
```

Use it to answer "how far apart are we, and on which side?" in one command. Two `<` lines = behind 2, three `>` lines = ahead 3, which matches `git status -sb`.

examples.description: Show both sides of a divergence, marked < (remote only) and > (local only).
Same, drawn as a graph.

subtoc.author: mike-rambil

subtoc.Name: git diff: Two-Dot vs Three-Dot
subtoc.short_description: Two-dot diff compares two snapshots. Three-dot diff shows only B's changes since it diverged from A.
subtoc.long_description:
`git diff` compares **snapshots**, not commit lists, so the dots mean something different here than in `git log`.

**`git diff A..B`** is identical to `git diff A B`: a straight comparison of the two tips. Red `-` lines exist in A but not in B, and green `+` lines are new in B. **Caveat:** if A has its own newer commits, their content shows up as red "deletions", even though B never deleted anything. B just doesn't have it yet.

**`git diff A...B`** diffs from the **merge base** of A and B to B. It shows only what B changed since the branches split, and ignores whatever happened on A. This is what a GitHub pull request's "Files changed" tab shows.

```
        A1──A2          ← A
       /
──M───
       \
        B1──B2          ← B

git diff A..B   →  A2 vs B2
git diff A...B  →  M  vs B2
```

In the demo repo, the teammate's `teammate.txt` appears as a deletion with two dots, and disappears with three:

```
$ git diff --stat origin/main..main
 app.txt      | 1 +
 feature.txt  | 2 ++
 teammate.txt | 2 --          ← not deleted by you, you just don't have it yet
 3 files changed, 3 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

$ git diff --stat origin/main...main
 app.txt     | 1 +
 feature.txt | 2 ++
 2 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
```

examples.description: Only your changes since you branched off origin/main (PR-style).
Exact difference between the two tips (what main would look like vs. origin/main).

examples.code: git diff $(git merge-base origin/main main) main
examples.description: Long form of the three-dot diff.

warnings: Don't read red lines in a two-dot diff as "I deleted this" when you're behind. Check `git status -sb` or use three dots.
subtoc.author: mike-rambil

subtoc.Name: Two-Dot vs Three-Dot Cheat Sheet
subtoc.short_description: One table for all four combinations, plus when the two forms give the same answer.
subtoc.long_description:
| | `A..B` (two dots) | `A...B` (three dots) |
|---|---|---|
| **`git log`** | Commits in B, not in A | Commits in A or B, not both (add `--left-right` for `<` / `>`) |
| **`git diff`** | Snapshot A vs snapshot B (same as `git diff A B`) | merge-base(A, B) vs B: only B's changes since divergence |

**When do `..` and `...` agree?** When A is an ancestor of B, i.e. B is not behind A. Then the merge base *is* A, so `git diff A...B` equals `git diff A..B`, and A has no commits of its own, so `git log A...B` lists the same commits as `git log A..B`. In push terms: once you've pulled/rebased and `git status -sb` shows only `[ahead N]`, both forms give the same answer.
subtoc.author: mike-rambil

subtoc.Name: Pre-Push Safety Check Recipe
subtoc.short_description: Four commands to run before pushing to a branch other people also push to.
subtoc.long_description:
Run these in order before `git push`, especially on a shared branch like `main`:

```sh
git fetch origin && git status -sb               # 1. ahead/behind, against a fresh remote
git log --oneline origin/main..main             # 2. exactly which commits will be pushed
git diff --stat origin/main..main               # 3. which files those commits touch
git log --oneline --left-right origin/main...main  # 4. if diverged: who has what
```

- Only `[ahead N]`: step 2 lists the N commits you'll push. Review them and push.
- Any `behind`: pull first (`git pull --rebase` or merge), then rerun the checks. Until you do, step 3 will show the remote's new work as red deletions.
- Step 2 lists commits you didn't expect (another session, a stray WIP commit): stop and sort it out *before* they're public.
warnings: Once pushed, rewriting shared history needs a force-push. Prefer catching surprises here. If you must, use `git push --force-with-lease`.
protips: Swap `origin/main` for `@{u}` to make the recipe work on any branch with an upstream, e.g. `git log --oneline @{u}..`.
subtoc.author: mike-rambil

short_description: Restore or pull changes for specific files from a past commit without reverting the entire commit.
long_description: How to use git to pull or restore changes for only certain files from a specific commit, without affecting the rest of your working directory or reverting the whole commit. Useful for cherry-picking file-level changes.

examples.description: Restore file1.txt and file2.txt from the specified commit.

examples.code:
git add path/to/file1.txt path/to/file2.txt
git commit -m "Pulled changes for file1.txt and file2.txt from commit e8ab7f64"
git push origin revert/productionOrder
examples.description: Stage, commit, and push the restored files to a new branch.
Restore files using the newer 'git restore' command.

steps: Checkout the specific files from the desired commit using 'git checkout <commit-hash> -- <file1> <file2>'.
Stage the changes with 'git add <file1> <file2>'.
Commit the changes with a descriptive message.
Push your branch and create a pull request if needed.
warnings: This will overwrite the current working directory versions of the specified files.
Make sure to commit or stash any local changes to those files before running the command.
